Ronnie Milsap's Journey Begins - Today In Country Music History

RONNIE MILSAP WAS HEADED TOWARD LAW SCHOOL WHEN RAY CHARLES HEARD HIM PLAY AND TOLD HIM NOT TO WALK AWAY FROM THE MUSIC ALREADY INSIDE HIM. By then, Milsap had spent most of his childhood at North Carolina’s state school for the blind, where classical piano and violin were part of his education even as country, gospel, rhythm and blues slipped into his world through late-night radio. He later remembered counselors warning that trying to become a professional musician could leave him dependent on the state, advice that pushed practicality against the one thing he already knew how to do exceptionally well. After graduating in 1962, Milsap studied pre-law at Young Harris College and had a path toward continuing his education, but music kept pulling him elsewhere. While still a student, he met Ray Charles, his musical hero, and Charles encouraged him to trust that instinct rather than abandon it for a safer profession. Milsap’s own official biography remembers the advice simply: Charles could hear the music inside him. The decision did not deliver Nashville immediately. Milsap spent the next several years moving through Atlanta clubs, soul and R&B sessions, small labels and eventually Memphis, where he worked around Chips Moman’s American Studio and played piano on Elvis Presley’s “Kentucky Rain.” By the early 1970s he had already touched several corners of American popular music without yet finding the career that would define him. Charley Pride eventually urged him toward Nashville, and on December 26, 1972, Milsap arrived to headline the showroom at the King of the Road Hotel. The response was immediate enough that he had a manager within weeks and was recording for RCA within three months. What followed was not a narrow country career. Milsap carried soul phrasing, pop instincts and piano-driven arrangements into country radio, eventually scoring thirty-five Billboard No. 1 country hits while crossing repeatedly into pop and adult contemporary audiences. The safer path had once pointed toward law. The one he chose instead helped broaden what mainstream country could sound like in the 1970s and 1980s.
